inspection_summary: All 253 logical lines were inspected. The article gives, conditionally on the Riemann hypothesis, an improved prime-number-theorem remainder outside an exceptional set of finite logarithmic measure, short derivations of mean-value estimates, and a normal-density result for primes in short intervals. Its reusable proof architecture is readable at the prose level: truncate an explicit formula over zeta zeros, control low and high zero ranges in mean square, convert those controls into exceptional-set or averaged conclusions, and balance a truncation parameter. Displayed mathematics is substantially damaged by OCR, so exact formulas, powers, constants, and some function symbols are not treated as reliably recoverable from this artifact alone.

accepted_units.title: RH consequences organized by exceptional-set and mean-value strength
accepted_units.why_material: The introduction distinguishes three kinds of conditional information about the prime-number-theorem remainder: a sharper pointwise estimate away from a finite-logarithmic-measure set, global mean-value bounds, and an almost-everywhere consequence obtained from a mean-square estimate. It also says the strongest exceptional-set statement combines the mechanisms behind the baseline pointwise bound and the mean-square bound, exposing a transferable bridge from average control to rare-exception control.
accepted_units.context_note: This unit carries the article's main conceptual agenda and the relationship among the later arguments; it is not evidence beyond the paper's own conditional claims.
accepted_units.representation_dependency: The prose and the phrases 'finite logarithmic measure' and 'almost all' are legible, but OCR corrupts the displayed functions and exponents in formulas (1)-(4). Preserve the qualitative hierarchy and proof relationship only; verify exact notation and rates against a scan before formula-level use.

accepted_units.title: Normal density in growing short intervals and the role of pair-density information
accepted_units.why_material: The paper states an averaged normal-density conclusion for primes in increasing short intervals under a growth condition that makes the interval length dominate a logarithmic scale, then records that adding Montgomery-type pair-density information strengthens the earlier pointwise remainder estimate. This separates what RH supplies from what additional correlation information about zeros can buy.
accepted_units.context_note: The short-interval statement is proved in the final section; the comparison with the joint RH and pair-density hypothesis is contextual rather than part of that proof.
accepted_units.representation_dependency: The prose conditions that the interval-length function is increasing, smaller than the ambient variable, and grows faster than a logarithmic power are readable. The displayed integral, precise power, and little-o/big-O typography are OCR-damaged and should not be quoted exactly from this extraction.

accepted_units.title: Truncate the zero sum and dispose of the low-zero contribution
accepted_units.why_material: The argument reduces the prime-counting remainder to a truncated sum over complex zeta zeros plus a controlled error, then combines a unit-interval zero-count bound with a low-height cutoff to show that the low-zero range already meets the target scale. Conceptually, this isolates the high-zero range as the only part requiring an exceptional-set estimate.
accepted_units.context_note: This is the setup for the logarithmic exceptional-set argument on the following lines and is conditional on RH as declared by the paper.
accepted_units.representation_dependency: Formula (6) is severely garbled: the prime-counting symbol, zero summand, cutoff, and error typography are not reliable. Only the prose facts that the sum runs over zeros and that zeros in a unit-height interval are logarithmically bounded, together with the stated qualitative low-range conclusion, are safe here.

accepted_units.title: Mean-square zero-sum control yields finite logarithmic exceptional measure
accepted_units.why_material: A mean-square estimate for the remaining zero sum is converted into a bound for the logarithmic measure of points where that sum is too large. Applying the bound on exponentially spaced blocks and choosing the cutoff logarithmically makes the blockwise bad measures summable, which yields a total exceptional set of finite logarithmic measure. This is a substantive and reusable average-to-exceptional-set mechanism.
accepted_units.context_note: The conclusion is the paper's formula (2), reached after the low-zero treatment in the preceding unit; the exact inequality is less secure than the prose description of the block argument.
accepted_units.representation_dependency: Most of formulas (7) and the bad-set threshold are fragmented or reordered by OCR. The references to a large-sieve lemma, the interval [X,eX], the choice T=log X, exponential blocks, and finite total logarithmic measure are readable; exact integrands, denominators, and exponents require the scan.

accepted_units.title: Obtain the unweighted mean-square estimate by splitting
accepted_units.why_material: The second section explicitly says that specializing the preceding zero-sum estimate gives a normalized local mean-square bound and that a splitting-up argument then produces the global mean-square claim (3). It identifies how control on multiplicative-size blocks is aggregated into a longer-range estimate.
accepted_units.context_note: This compact bridge is the proof supplied for formula (3); it relies on formulas (6) and (7) rather than reproducing their estimates.
accepted_units.representation_dependency: The displayed formula (8) is OCR-corrupted, so its exact normalization and bound cannot be recovered confidently. The dependency on (6)-(7) and the splitting mechanism are clear in prose.

accepted_units.title: Choose a slowly growing cutoff to isolate the diagonal zero contribution
accepted_units.why_material: For the logarithmically weighted mean-value asymptotic, the paper first takes a fixed zero cutoff and identifies a leading contribution involving distinct zeros weighted by their multiplicities. It then lets the cutoff tend to infinity slowly enough that its logarithm is negligible relative to the ambient logarithm, uses the earlier mean-square estimate to make the omitted part lower order, and combines this with a companion bound to obtain formula (4). The move separates a finite spectral calculation from a controlled tail.
accepted_units.context_note: The constant in the asymptotic is represented through zero multiplicities in the damaged display; this unit records the limiting strategy and multiplicity role, not a reconstructed exact formula.
accepted_units.representation_dependency: Lines 115-150 contain severe symbol substitution and displaced formula fragments, including a trailing bound at line 150. The prose about distinct zeros, multiplicity, a suitable T tending to infinity, log T=o(log X), use of (7), and combination with (8) is reliable; exact sums, weights, and the constant must be scan-checked.

accepted_units.title: Decompose the short-interval remainder by zero-frequency range
accepted_units.why_material: The proof of the normal-density statement begins by applying the explicit formula to the difference across an interval. It reorganizes the result into an integral contribution and two auxiliary zero sums separated at a tunable height T, thereby exposing distinct pieces that can be bounded by different mean-square arguments.
accepted_units.context_note: The auxiliary functions named S1 and S2 in the OCR are subsequently estimated in the remainder of section 3; the decomposition is the structural entry point for that proof.
accepted_units.representation_dependency: The displayed definitions and decomposition are badly OCR-damaged, although the ranges below and above T, the constraints on the ambient point, interval length, and cutoff, and the prose 'this may be written as' remain visible. Do not infer exact signs, powers, or summands without the page image.

accepted_units.title: Control each decomposed term and balance the truncation at the interval scale
accepted_units.why_material: The final argument bounds the integral piece through a zero-sum integral estimate, controls the two boundary terms by the earlier mean-square result, assembles a parameter-dependent mean-square inequality, and chooses the cutoff in terms of the ambient scale and interval length. Under the stated growth condition on the interval length, the assembled bound is little-o of the target scale; a final splitting-up argument completes the normal-density conclusion.
accepted_units.context_note: This unit closes the proof of (5) and shows that the earlier exceptional-set machinery also serves a short-interval averaged problem after a different parameter balance.
accepted_units.representation_dependency: Nearly every display in lines 176-221 is fragmented, and the OCR confuses variables in the final cutoff and growth condition. The sequence of bounding steps, reuse of (7), monotonicity of the interval-length function, parameter choice, and little-o conclusion are readable, but the precise inequality and cutoff formula require verification from the scan.

within_source_synthesis_candidates.title: A shared truncation-and-averaging template for exceptional sets and short intervals
within_source_synthesis_candidates.claim: Both headline applications begin from a truncated explicit formula over zeta zeros, split the spectral contribution at a tunable scale, use mean-square control to suppress the difficult range, and select the scale to match the desired notion of rarity: summability of logarithmic bad-set measure in the pointwise application and a little-o averaged error in the short-interval application.
within_source_synthesis_candidates.limit: This is a synthesis of the source's proof organization, not a claim that the two displayed calculations are identical. Because the formulas are OCR-damaged, exact cutoffs, exponents, and normalization cannot be compared from this artifact alone.

within_source_synthesis_candidates.title: Spectral truncation as a bridge from zero information to prime-counting statistics
within_source_synthesis_candidates.claim: Across pointwise exceptional-set, global mean-value, and short-interval results, the paper treats information about zeros as useful through controlled truncations and averaged estimates; multiplicity and pair-density information mark two distinct ways that finer zero statistics can sharpen prime-counting conclusions.
within_source_synthesis_candidates.limit: The pair-density comparison is only reported in the introduction and is not derived in this article, while the multiplicity formula is not reliably legible in OCR. The synthesis therefore remains qualitative and conditional.
